items.title: Force methods vs structural methods vs DNA-spring chimeras
items.cap: Schematic: what each approach can measure

points.text: Single-molecule force methods (optical and magnetic tweezers, AFM) apply and measure force, but read out only one end-to-end distance, not the structure
Structural methods (cryoEM, X-ray) give atomic structures, but of proteins at rest, with no force applied
Our approach: attach a DNA spring to the protein (sfGFP, PP2A) across two chosen residues, so the spring itself applies the force
Every molecule carries its own spring, so a whole sample is under load and can be frozen for cryoEM: force and atomic structure simultaneously, which the traditional single-molecule methods cannot do

slides.title: Three kinds of DNA spring, and why we need all three

items.cap: Schematic of the three chimeras used throughout

points.text: ssDNA: a single strand is floppy, so it exerts little force on the two attachment sites
dsDNA (ssDNA + its complementary strand, cDNA): the stiff duplex must bend, so it pushes the sites apart much harder
Nicked dsDNA: the cDNA has one break in its backbone. Same DNA on the protein, but the nick relieves bending stress, so it delivers less force

Why it matters: the three carry similar amounts of DNA but different forces. Used as controls in the results that follow, a change seen only with the stronger spring is due to force, not to steric hindrance from simply having DNA there

slides.q: How a spectrofluorometer records excitation and emission spectra

items.title: Fluorometer schematic
items.cap: Animated schematic of the Fluorolog-3 light path; spectrum shapes are sketches of sfGFP’s known spectra

points.text: Instrument: HORIBA Jobin Yvon Fluorolog-3. Xe lamp → excitation monochromator (picks the colour that hits the sample) → cuvette → emission monochromator at 90° (picks the colour counted) → detector S1; a reference photodiode R1 tracks the lamp
Excitation spectrum: hold the detected wavelength at 510 nm and sweep the excitation 400→500 nm. It shows which colours the chromophore absorbs and turns into fluorescence
Emission spectrum: hold the excitation at 485 nm and sweep the detected wavelength 500→600 nm. It shows what colour, and how much, light comes out
485 nm and 510 nm are sfGFP’s known excitation and emission maxima. The small 400 nm band is the neutral chromophore: it is the basis of our band ratio

slides.title: What the band ratio measures
slides.q: 1-tet sfGFP concentration series, 2026-08-25

items.cap: Mean of 3 scans per concentration · raw counts, linear y · excitation S1 ÷ R1 (lamp-corrected), emission S1
Same data on a log y-axis · inset: I(peak) vs concentration, log–log

explain.text: Two spectra per sample, on one wavelength axis (raw counts, linear y). Left (solid, left y-axis): excitation spectra, detecting at 510 nm while the excitation sweeps 400 → 500 nm; lamp-corrected as S1 ÷ R1. Right (dashed, right y-axis): emission spectra, exciting at 485 nm while the detected wavelength sweeps 500 → 600 nm. Colour = concentration, light (2 µM) to dark (32 µM), labelled on each curve.

points.text: Band ratio = I(400) / I(peak), both read off the excitation spectrum
I(peak) (circles): the excitation maximum, 484–486 nm: the anionic chromophore band
I(400) (squares): the excitation intensity at 400 nm: the neutral chromophore band

▶ I now switch to a log y-axisHeadline: fluorescence is not linear in concentration: 16× more protein (2 → 32 µM) gives only 11× more I(peak). Our samples were not all at the same concentration, so we cannot simply rescale raw intensities: we need a concentration-independent metric

How the log plot shows it (box on the plot): each doubling should lift a curve by the same step; 2 → 4 → 8 µM do, 8 → 16 → 32 µM rise less and less (×1.8, ×1.4), and the inset’s measured I(peak) falls below the proportional line
The band ratio is that metric: I(400) and I(peak) come from the same spectrum, so concentration cancels; it stays at 0.097–0.105 from 2 to 8 µM

slides.intro:
So we want to measure fluorescence. What metric do we use?

Presenting: the band ratio

slides.title: Concentration ladder - inner filter effect

callouts.html: What justifies the use of band ratio as our fluorometry metric?

Inner filter effect: at high concentration the sample itself absorbs much of the excitation light before it reaches the centre of the cuvette, where the detector looks. The more strongly a wavelength is absorbed, the more of it is lost: sfGFP absorbs strongly at its 485 nm peak but only weakly at 400 nm. Literature: noticeable from ≈ 5 µM; here the ratio is flat to 8 µM and rises from 16 µM.

What it does to the band ratio\frac{I(400)\;{\color{#2e7d4f}\approx}}{I(\text{peak})\;{\color{#b8372c}\downarrow}} = \text{ratio}\;{\color{#b86e00}\Uparrow}I(peak) ↓: 485 nm light is absorbed most, so less of it excites the observed volume
I(400) ≈: weakly absorbed, barely affected
⇒ ratio ↑, as at 16 and 32 µMLakowicz, Principles of Fluorescence Spectroscopy, 3rd ed., Springer (2006), ch. 2; Kubista et al., Analyst 119, 417 (1994)

slides.title: What is MD analysis? How?

points.text:
Ramachandran plots
  • Does the addition of tet groups significantly affect the structural conformation of our protein?

Backbone rigidity: RMSF
  • To what extent does the spring deform the entire scaffold? Does the overall structural integrity of the protein still persist?

Forces applied: direct force field + modelled forces
  • How much force can we actually transmit to the protein via the DNA springs?
  • Do theoretical models of force agree with the forces measured in the MD force field?

DNA dynamics
  • Is the DNA kinked, or coiled up (under torsion), which would then affect DNA-spring force application?
  • Is the DNA otherwise interacting with the protein, other than applying direct mechanical force?

aside.html:
Recap: MD goals
  • Force modelling (to make the system reproducible and configurable to different proteins)
  • Suitability of a candidate protein for study under a DNA spring

slides.title: sfGFP MD: the protein and the simulated systems

items.cap: Structure: what each part is
Overview: barrel, two Tet2-Et/sTCO tethers, 27 bp duplex
Strain: putty tube scaled by per-residue RMSF
Chromophore: the three H-bonds that stop it twisting

explain.text: sfGFP architecture (238 residues). β-strands: extended segments hydrogen-bonded side by side; eleven of them form the β-barrel wall (≈ 42 Å tall, 24 Å across), the rigid part. A central α-helix threads the barrel axis and carries the chromophore (made from Thr65–Tyr66–Gly67), sealed off from solvent; short helices also sit on the caps. Loops: the short, irregular segments that join one strand to the next at the two ends (caps) of the barrel. Nothing holds them in the sheet, so they are the most mobile parts (e.g. residues 189–194 between strands 9 and 10).

The spring. Our tethers (orange, Tet2-Et clicked to sTCO) attach at Asp133 and Asn149 (red), 31.3 Å apart across the barrel, with His148, which bonds the chromophore, between them. The DNA spring (blue) spans the two tethers and pushes or pulls on the sites.

points.text: Sites: Asp133 and Asn149, 31.3 Å apart, with His148 between them bonded to the chromophore
Systems compared: WT sfGFP · tethers unclicked vs clicked (no DNA, the zero) · DNA springs of various lengths · dsDNA vs ssDNA · intact vs nicked duplex · a direct force clamp
Animations show the 27 bp spring chimera (50 ns, water stripped, superposed on the barrel core)
Scale: 4,050 ns of production, 81 replicates across 17 systems

slides.title: sfGFP: backbone rigidity (RMSF)
slides.q: Is the backbone rigid, with and without force?

items.cap: Cα RMSF, aligned on the barrel core
Axial force clamp on the unclicked protein

explain.text: RMSF (root-mean-square fluctuation): how far each residue’s Cα atom wanders from its own average position over the trajectory, after every frame is aligned on the rigid core. Low = rigid, high = mobile. x-axis: residue number (2B3P numbering); y-axis: Cα RMSF (Å). Dashed lines mark the chromophore (CRO 66) and the attachment sites Asp133, His148, Asn149. One colour per system. The low, flat stretches (≈ 0.4 Å) are the β-strands of the barrel wall. The peaks are loops, the short connectors between strands at the barrel caps: the tallest is residues 189–194 (between strands 9 and 10, ≈ 1.5 Å), then 155–158 and 211–212.

<dfn>Axial force clamp</dfn>: a constant force F applied directly between the Cβ atoms of Asp133 and Asn149 of the unclicked protein, pulling them apart, with no DNA: a controlled stand-in for a spring. x-axis: F (pN); y-axis: Cβ–Cβ distance (Å), mean ± sem of 3 replicates. Shaded: ±0.5 Å around the unloaded (0 pN) distance.

points.text: The β-barrel stays uniformly rigid (≈ 0.4 Å on the strands) in every system, including WT with no force at all
RMSF traces overlie each other; only the loops and the tethers move
With no force, the site distance is 31.61 ± 0.07 Å: the unloaded barrel barely fluctuates
0 → 20 pN shifts it by only 0.14 Å; the 4 pN dip is replicate noise. Compliance 0.0105 ± 0.0057 Å/pN (includes zero), so κ > 107 kBT nm⁻²
Answer: the backbone is already super rigid without any force, and force barely changes it

slides.title: Kinked vs unkinked DNA: how the shape sets the force
slides.q: Same duplex, same end-to-end distance; only how the bend is distributed differs

items.title: Kinked vs unkinked duplex
items.cap: Schematic: 27 bp duplex at x = 68 Å; forces from Zocchi’s model (B = 200 pN nm², τ<sub>c</sub> = 34 pN nm)

points.text: Both ends are held closer than the duplex’s length (x < L), so the duplex must bend. The question is where the bending goes

Unkinked (Zocchi’s Euler-buckling picture): the bend is shared by every base-pair step, a few degrees each. Every step is strained, the whole rod stores bending energy, and it pushes back on the ends with ≈ π²B/L² (≈ 24 pN for 27 bp)
Kinked: one step breaks sharply (base stacking lost, often a pair opened) while the two arms stay straight and relaxed. Almost all the bending sits in one spot
Effect on force transduction: a kink acts as a release valve. The relaxed arms store almost no energy, so the push is capped by the kink’s critical torque τc: only ≈ 5–7 pN reaches the protein

Squeeze the ends closer: the smooth rod keeps pushing at ≈ its Euler load; the kinked rod stays weak. So whether the DNA kinks decides whether the spring delivers tens of pN or a few. Next: does our DNA kink in MD, and what does Zocchi’s model predict?

slides.q: What is simulated, what each variable means, and how the force is read off

items.title: Bare duplex restraint simulation
items.cap: Animated schematic of the MD set-up; readout values are real 27 bp runs (stiff restraint)

points.text: System: bare dsDNA duplex (two base-paired strands) in water, no protein
L: length along the helix, 89 Å (27 bp)
x₀: rest length of a virtual spring on the ends, set by us; x₀ < L forces a bend
x(t): end-to-end distance now; jiggles ≈ ±1 Å by thermal motion at 300 K, not by any kick
⟨x⟩: time average of x(t); the spring stretches to it, so f = k(⟨x⟩ − x₀)
Fixed? Yes per run (x within ≈ 1 Å); one run = one point (⟨x⟩, f)
Zocchi: predicts f(x) from B (bending stiffness) and τc (kink torque)
Below xc the model kinks: arms of length R, push of a few pN

slides.q: Is the DNA kinked or coiled? Does it interact with the protein beyond pushing?

items.cap: Axis bend per base-pair step in the MD chimeras (zoomed: 0–10°)
Same profiles with a kinked duplex overlaid (0–100°)

explain.text: x-axis: base pair along the duplex; y-axis: <dfn>axis bend</dfn> at each base-pair step (°), the angle between the helix axes either side of it. Mean of 6 runs per chimera. Zoomed to 0–10°, the profiles look jagged: but is any of this a <dfn>kink</dfn>, a sharp break at one step?

points.text: Zoomed in, the MD profiles look spiky: steps vary between 3 and 8°
Now overlay what a kinked duplex would look like at the same end-to-end distance (Zocchi’s kinked rod): 51° (27 bp) and 76° (40 bp) at one step, 0° elsewhere
On the same axis the MD “spikes” vanish into the 0–10° band: the duplex bends smoothly, 4.8–5.2°/bp on average, with no kink
The DNA touches the protein in 72–98 % of frames: local contact, not action at a distance
Answer: no kink and no coiling; the DNA bends smoothly and lies against the protein

slides.title: Why Zocchi’s model puts our springs in the kinked regime

Lcontour length along the helix, 0.33 nm × Nbp (8.9 nm for 27 bp)
Bbending stiffness of dsDNA, ≈ 200 pN nm²
τccritical torque: bending torque at which one base-pair step gives way and the duplex kinks (34 pN nm; 27 if nicked)
γkink parameter Lτc/2B: how close the rod is to kinking
xccritical end-to-end distance: below it, the rod kinks
κccritical curvature τc/B: bending per length at which kinking starts
xMDend-to-end distance of the duplex in our chimera MD, 63–73 Å
Reffective arm length of the kinked rod
fkinkedpush of the kinked rod on its ends

slides.q: Zocchi’s equations (Molecular Machines §2.15) evaluated with our MD numbers

points.text: Inputs: Zocchi’s parameters; in our chimera MD the ends sit x = 63–73 Å apart, bent 4.8–5.2°/bpL = 0.33\,\mathrm{nm}\times N_{\mathrm{bp}}, \qquad B = k_BT\,\ell_p \approx 200\ \mathrm{pN\,nm^2}, \qquad \tau_c = 34\ (\text{intact}),\ 27\ (\text{nicked})\ \mathrm{pN\,nm}

Step 1: the kink parameter (eq. 2.194)\gamma = \frac{L\,\tau_c}{2B} = \frac{8.91 \times 34}{2 \times 200} = 0.76\ \ (27\ \text{bp}), \qquad \frac{13.2 \times 34}{2 \times 200} = 1.12\ \ (40\ \text{bp})

Step 2: the critical distance (eq. 2.188), compared with our MD distancesx_c = L\Big(1-\frac{\gamma^2}{15}\Big) = 86\ \text{Å}\ (27\ \text{bp}),\ 121\ \text{Å}\ (40\ \text{bp}) \;>\; x_{\mathrm{MD}} = 63\text{–}73\ \text{Å} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{kinked regime}

Same from curvature: kinking starts once the bending torque Bκ reaches τc\kappa_c = \frac{\tau_c}{B} = \frac{34}{200}\ \text{nm}^{-1} \;\Rightarrow\; \kappa_c \times 0.33\ \tfrac{\text{nm}}{\text{bp}} = 3.2^\circ/\text{bp}\ \ (2.6^\circ/\text{bp nicked}) \;<\; 4.8\text{–}5.2^\circ/\text{bp in the MD}

So the model predicts the kinked-branch force (eq. 2.196):f_{\mathrm{kinked}}(x) = \frac{\tau_c}{2R\sqrt{1-(x/2R)^2}},\quad R = \frac{L}{2}\Big(1-\frac{\gamma^2}{90}\Big) \;\Rightarrow\; 5.5\text{–}6.8\ \text{pN}\ (27\ \text{bp}),\ \ 3.0\text{–}3.2\ \text{pN}\ (40\ \text{bp})
Headline: our chimeras hold the duplex at 63–73 Å, below xc = 86 Å (27 bp) and 121 Å (40 bp). Zocchi’s model therefore puts them in the kinked regime and predicts only ≈ 3–7 pN

Main ideaZocchi’s model has a threshold torque τc: once bending exceeds it, DNA must kink, and the push collapses to a few pN.

The MD force field has no such threshold. A kink could only emerge from base pairs actually breaking, which did not happen at 4.8–5.2°/bp, so the simulated duplex stays unkinked and keeps pushing at tens of pN.

items.cap: Zocchi’s force against end-to-end distance, both branches
Zocchi recomputed at the force field’s own distances

explain.text: Zocchi’s model (calculation): push f against imposed end-to-end distance x, for 27 and 40 bp. Solid unkinked, dotted kinked, dashed unkinked continued below xc; grey band = our chimeras (63–73 Å).
Model vs MD at the ⟨x⟩ each bare duplex sat at: grey kinked prediction, light blue unkinked prediction, dark blue MD force k(⟨x⟩ − x₀) (mean ± sem; dots = runs).

points.text: Kinked regime (x < xc): the kink takes up the bending, so the push collapses to a few pN
Unkinked regime: the push stays near the Euler load π²B/L² ≈ 10B/L² (24.9 pN for 27 bp, 11.3 pN for 40 bp), almost independent of x
Our chimeras (grey band) sit well inside the kinked regime of the model: 5× less force than if the rod stays unkinked

TakeawayOnce the kinking condition is removed, Zocchi’s model and the MD force field are much more in agreement: 24.1 vs 28.0, 13.9 vs 15.8 and 11.9 vs 13.2 pN, within 1.1–1.2×.

slides.title: sfGFP: why fluorometry saw no change across ss, ds and nicked
slides.q: Excitation/emission wavelengths and band ratio barely moved. Does the MD explain it?

items.cap: Chromophore (green) inside the barrel with the 27 bp spring attached; dashed: its three key H-bonds
Occupancy of each chromophore H-bond, per system (ticks = replicates, filled = mean)

explain.text: What sets the colour and brightness. The chromophore (CRO 66) is buried in the β-barrel and held flat by a hydrogen-bond network: Thr203 and His148 to the phenolate oxygen, Arg96 and Gln94 to the imidazolinone carbonyl. Its excitation/emission wavelengths depend on this electrostatic environment and its protonation state; its brightness drops if it can twist about the two bonds of the methine bridge (a free chromophore is essentially dark). His148 sits between the two attachment sites, the mechanical path from the spring to the fluorophore.

Each row is one hydrogen bond around the chromophore; x-axis: <dfn>occupancy</dfn>, the % of frames in which the bond is formed (H···acceptor < 2.5 Å and angle > 120°). Ticks are individual replicates, filled symbols the means; one colour per system (WT, 2× Tet2-Et, clicked no DNA, 27 / 40 / 40-nicked bp springs). If a spring were prising the barrel open near the chromophore, the load-bearing bonds would fall.

points.text: Load-bearing bonds hold in every system: Arg96 100 %, Thr203 96–97 %, Gln94 92–97 %
His148 → phenolate: 72 % (WT) vs 72–82 % with springs, inside its own 39–92 % replicate scatter
Chromophore planarity unchanged: bridge twists τ 5.1–5.6°, φ 6.0–6.5° in all systems; cavity water 9–11 molecules
The barrel is stiff: RMSF ≈ 0.4 Å on the strands, κ > 107 k<sub>B</sub>T nm⁻² (0 → 20 pN moves the sites 0.14 Å, RMSF slide)
Answer: the springs never deform the chromophore’s environment, so no wavelength shift or band-ratio change is expected; seeing one would need a softer site or far stronger force

Main resultThe crucial hydrogen bonds around the chromophore (Arg96, Thr203, Gln94) stay at ≈ 92–100 % occupancy with or without a spring.

Further proof that our springs cannot meaningfully perturb the chromophore, on top of the rigid sfGFP backbone shown earlier (slide 16).

slides.eqbox:
How occupancy was computed (MD simulations/sfGFP/analysis/chromophore.py, mdtraj)
dh  = md.compute_distances(t, [[h, acc] ...])
ang = md.compute_angles(t, [[don, h, acc] ...])
occ = ((d_HA < 2.5) & (ang > 120)).mean()
Formed when dHA < 2.5 Å and ang > 120°; occupancy = fraction of frames formed.
Why these two numbers: the H on an electronegative donor carries a partial + charge and is pulled by a lone pair (δ−) on the acceptor. That attraction is only strong when H sits close to A and the D–H points straight at it (≈ 180°), so a short dHA and a near-linear angle mean a real H-bond.

slides.title: Why add DTT? Favouring the 1 : 1 circle
slides.q: Breaking disulfide bonds so each pp2a reacts on its own

items.title: DTT and intra- vs intermolecular click
items.cap: Schematic (not to scale): red = pp2a A subunit, green = Tet sites, blue = DNA, yellow = disulfide

points.text: Without DTT, cysteines on neighbouring pp2a form disulfide (S–S) bonds: the proteins stick together
A DNA strand can then click across two proteins (intermolecular), giving 2 pp2a + 2 DNA products
DTT reduces S–S to two free –SH groups, so the proteins separate
Each DNA strand can now only close on its own protein (intramolecular): the 1 pp2a + 1 DNA circle
Expected: more 1 : 1 circular product, less 2 : 2 (next slide tests it)

Problem: click chemistry is still inhibited even after desalting (right gel). Left gel: find the minimum DTT that still reduces all or most disulfide bonds, so as little DTT as possible is carried over.

slides.intro:

slides.title: PP2A architecture: A, C and B subunits
slides.q: PP2A works as a three-subunit holoenzyme: scaffold A, catalytic C, regulatory B

items.title: PP2A architecture: A, C and B subunits
items.cap: Schematic (not to scale)

points.text: A, scaffold (PPP2R1A/B, ≈ 65 kDa): a horseshoe of 15 HEAT repeats with no activity of its own; it holds the other two in place
C, catalytic (PPP2CA/B): the phosphatase itself; binds HEAT 11–15. A + C = the AC core dimer, which forms first. Its C-terminal tail (methylated at Leu309) helps B bind
B, regulatory: binds the AC core on HEAT 1–10 to complete the ABC holoenzyme. 4 families (B55, B56, PR72, striatin), > 40 isoforms; B decides which substrate and where in the cell

slides.intro:
Now that our gels give at least some evidence of a circular product, it makes sense to start thinking about the next step: designing assays that test the physiological function of PP2A under spring attachment.

Before that, we first need to understand the key features of PP2A.

items.title: [Plans] B56-binding assay: biolayer interferometry (BLI)
items.cap: Schematic of BLI; curves computed from Day et al.’s fitted rate constants (Fig. 5B, B56α); timings illustrative

points.text: Biosensor: an optical-fibre tip coated with B56 (AR2G tip, amine coupling). Bound mass shifts the reflected light by Δλ
Baseline in buffer: nothing binds
Association: dip into the AC core dimer (31–500 nM); AC binds B56 and Δλ rises, at a rate set by kon
Dissociation: back into buffer; AC falls off and Δλ decays, at a rate set by koff
Fit (1:1 binding):AC + B \;\xrightleftharpoons[k_{\mathrm{off}}]{\;k_{\mathrm{on}}\;}\; ABC, \qquad K_D = \frac{k_{\mathrm{off}}}{k_{\mathrm{on}}}smaller KD = tighter binding
Day et al. result: Aβ binds B56 more weakly than Aα, KD 119.9 vs 25.7 nM for B56α (≈ 4.7×) and 14.0 vs 9.2 nM for B56γ (≈ 1.5×)
For us: measure KD for B56 binding to the Aα(+ spring)–C core vs the WT Aα–C core: does the spring weaken holoenzyme formation?

items.title: [Plans] Phosphatase activity assay (DiFMUP)
items.cap: Schematic of the assay; curves computed from Day et al.’s fitted K_M and V_max (Fig. S4D)

points.text: Enzyme: assembled holoenzyme, 20 nM AC core with excess (200 nM) B56γ
Substrate DiFMUP is dark; PP2A removes its phosphate → DiFMU, which fluoresces blue
The initial slope of fluorescence vs time is the velocity v at that substrate concentration
Repeat at 2–128 µM (triplicate) and fit Michaelis–Menten:v = \frac{V_{\max}\,[S]}{K_M + [S]}
Day et al. result: same activity for Aα and Aβ, KM 25.6 vs 34.9 µM and Vmax 60.1 vs 56.8 fluorescence/s, despite their different B56 binding
For us: the same assay on the Aα holoenzyme with and without the DNA spring: does the spring change its raw dephosphorylation capacity?

slides.title: Summary: what each assay tells us about our DNA-spring chimeras

points.text:
AssayWhat it can tell us about our DNA-spring chimeras
cryoEMAscertain spring attachment, and quantify the structural deformation physically
BLI bindingInvestigate holoenzyme formation (AC core + B), which is required for in vivo activity
Phosphatase activity
(DiFMUP)		Direct investigation of physiological function, using an artificial substrate
Why isn’t the phosphatase activity assay enough? Why also run BLI?
DiFMUP only needs the AC core (A + C): it does not require the B subunit. It is also an artificial substrate, unlike the real substrates PP2A meets in vivo, which B docks next to C
So DiFMUP measures the raw dephosphorylation capacity of our chimeras, independent of regulation by the B subunit as in real in vivo contexts. BLI covers that missing piece: does B still bind?

slides.title: cryoEM downstream analysis: how it differs from X-ray crystallography

items.title: cryoEM downstream analysis: how it differs from X-ray crystallography
items.cap: Animation drawn for this deck from the content of the cryoEM slides

points.text:
X-ray crystallographycryoEM
RadiationDiffracted X-ray photonsScattered and transmitted electron waves
3D reconstructionRecover missing Fourier phases → electron-density mapRecover particle orientations → electrostatic-potential map
RefinementReciprocal space: adjust atoms to match the measured diffraction intensitiesReal space: adjust atoms to fit the reconstructed 3D map

Both fit an atomic model into their reconstructed 3D maps.

Key differencesBoth X-ray crystallography and cryo-EM measure intensities rather than phases directly. However, unlike X-ray crystallography, where Fourier phase information is lost from diffraction intensity measurements, cryo-EM exploits electron-wave interference to encode phase information into detectable image intensity contrast.

Furthermore, whereas proteins in X-ray crystals form an ordered lattice, individual proteins in cryo-EM are randomly oriented in vitreous ice. Consequently, cryo-EM requires computational estimation of particle orientations to reconstruct a 3D structural map, whereas X-ray crystallography primarily requires recovering missing Fourier phases.

slides.title: What does it mean to defocus a lens?
slides.q: Thin lens: 1/f = 1/s + 1/s′, with the object and the sensor fixed

items.title: What does it mean to defocus a lens?
items.cap: Animation drawn for this deck from the content of the cryoEM slides

points.text: Stronger lens (shorter f): the rays cross before the sensor and spread into a disc
Weaker lens (longer f): the rays would meet beyond the sensor; again a disc. In the TEM this is underfocus
The objective lens current sets f, so turning the focus knob moves the focus by Δf. cryoEM images are taken deliberately ≈ 0.5–3 µm out of focus

slides.intro:
I will now try to explain the CryoSPARC downstream analysis in a hopefully intuitive way, as that is the software I have mainly been working with: essentially, how we get from 2D images to a 3D density map.

Crystallographers can hopefully draw parallels with reconstruction in X-ray crystallography, as some concepts are common to the two workflows: diffraction, and its connection to Fourier space.

slides.title: Effect 1: the protein shifts the phase AND absorbs amplitude (intensity)
slides.q: What happens to the electron beam as it passes through protein?

items.title: Effect 1: the protein shifts the phase AND absorbs amplitude (intensity)
items.cap: Animation drawn for this deck from the content of the cryoEM slides (phase shift exaggerated)

points.text: An amplitude object absorbs electrons: the wave leaves weaker, and the image is darker there
A phase object keeps the amplitude but delays the wave by φ (amplitude decrease is minor; the phase shift dominates)
A protein in ice is almost a pure phase object, and the detector records |ψ|² = |eiφ|² = 1: in focus it is nearly invisible

slides.title: Effect 2: the protein scatters the wave (diffraction)
slides.q: Where does each spatial frequency go?

items.title: Effect 2: the protein scatters the wave (diffraction)
items.cap: Animation drawn for this deck from the content of the cryoEM slides

points.text: A repeat of spacing d scatters the wave by α ≈ λ/d (Bragg: 2d sin θ = λ, with α = 2θ)
Finer detail scatters further: the direction encodes the spatial frequency q = 1/d
The objective lens sends each direction to one point of its back focal plane: fine detail lands far from the centre
At 300 kV (λ = 0.0197 Å) even 3 Å detail scatters by only ≈ 0.4°

slides.title: Key assumption: the weak phase object approximation
slides.q: Implication: the scattered wave is always 90° out of phase with the unscattered wave

aside.html:
Also implies the amplitude of the exit wave after scattering at the protein remains at unity, so there is no contrast between the unscattered reference and the scattered wave: the detector only picks up intensity, not the phase difference!I(x,y) = \big|e^{i\phi(x,y)}\big|^2 = 1
Drawn to scale for φ = 0.2 rad
Intensity of the exit wave (what the detector records):
I_{\mathrm{exit}} = |1 + i\phi|^2 = (1 + i\phi)(1 - i\phi) = 1 + \phi^2 = 1.04
Iexit ≈ 1 = Iunscattered: the exit wave is as bright as the unscattered reference, so the protein gives no contrast

points.text: Incident plane wave:\Psi_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathbf r, z) = e^{ikz}, \qquad k = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}
Exit wave after the protein:\Psi_{\mathrm{exit}}(x,y) = e^{i\phi(x,y)}Under the WPOA, |\phi| \ll 1, so a Taylor expansion givese^{i\phi} \approx 1 + i\phi
Therefore,\Psi_{\mathrm{exit}}(x,y) \approx 1 + i\phi(x,y)where 1 is the unscattered reference and iφ(x, y) is the scattered wave
Because i = e^{i\pi/2}, this perturbation is in quadrature (90° out of phase) with the reference, when φ is real

Under this approximation1. The scattered wave always differs in phase from the unscattered wave by π/2.

2. Their sum, the exit wave, is virtually indistinguishable in intensity from a wave that never passed through a protein, so we cannot see the protein yet.

slides.intro:
We saw that when the beam passes through the protein its phase shifts, the protein is then not visible on a detector that measures intensity.

(1) How is that so?
(2) How much is the phase of each beam that passed through the protein (scattered) shifted, relative to the unscattered beam?

It turns out the analysis simplifies greatly once we know that this phase shift is SMALL.

slides.title: Key principle: defocus turns phase shifts into contrast
slides.q: How do we make the scattered wave visible?

items.title: Key principle: defocus turns phase shifts into contrast
items.cap: Animation drawn for this deck from the content of the cryoEM slides (φ exaggerated)

points.text: Extra phase χ = π/2: the scattered wave becomes antiparallel to the reference, so the particle is dark
χ = 3π/2: parallel, so the particle is bright (contrast reversed)
Contrast ≈ −2φ sin χ: sin χ is the contrast transfer function, largest at χ = π/2 + kπ
Defocus supplies χ(q) = πλΔf q² − ½πC<sub>s</sub>λ³q⁴: a different extra phase for every spatial frequency q

Exit-wave intensity, scattered wave along the reference or at 90°:
antiparallel(1-\phi)^2 = 1 - 2\phi + \phi^2 \approx 1 - 2\phi
parallel(1+\phi)^2 = 1 + 2\phi + \phi^2 \approx 1 + 2\phi
perpendicular|1+i\phi|^2 = 1 + \phi^2 \approx 1
Under the WPOA \phi \ll 1, so to first order \phi^2 \approx 0 while 2\phi is not: only the parallel and antiparallel cases move the intensity away from unity, giving contrast. At 90° (in focus) the change is second order: invisible

slides.intro:
Adjusting the defocus changes the relative phase shift between the scattered and unscattered waves.

That is what creates the image contrast we need to see our protein.

slides.title: Where the defocus phase comes from: the Fresnel propagator
slides.q: Why does defocus give each spatial frequency q its own extra phase?

aside.html:
Terms
\psi(\mathbf r)electron wavefunction (complex amplitude) at position \mathbf r = (x, y, z)
z;\ x, yoptic axis (beam direction); transverse image-plane coordinates
\mathbf k = (k_x, k_y, k_z)wavevector: points along the direction of travel
\mathbf k_\perp,\ k_ztransverse (tilt off the axis) and axial components of \mathbf k
k_0 = 2\pi/\lambdawavenumber: length of \mathbf k, fixed by the beam energy
\lambdaelectron wavelength (0.0197 Å at 300 kV, so λq ≪ 1 for q ≲ 0.5 Å⁻¹)
\mathbf q = (q_x, q_y),\ q2D spatial frequency of a specimen detail (Å⁻¹) and its magnitude
H_z(q)Fresnel propagator: phase picked up over a distance z
\Delta fdefocus (positive = underfocus); sign conventions differ between texts
\chi_{\text{def}}(q)extra phase from defocus
C_sspherical-aberration coefficient: adds -\tfrac12\pi C_s\lambda^3 q^4

points.text: A 3D plane wave of wavelength λ travels along its wavevector \mathbf k. Specimen detail of spatial frequency \mathbf q scatters it off the optic axis z, giving it a transverse part \mathbf k_\perp\psi(\mathbf r) = e^{\,i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r} = e^{\,i(k_x x + k_y y + k_z z)}, \qquad \mathbf k_\perp = (k_x, k_y) = 2\pi\mathbf q

Elastic scattering keeps the energy, so |\mathbf k| = k_0 is unchanged. Solve for k_z and expand for small angles (\lambda q \ll 1):k_z^2 + |\mathbf k_\perp|^2 = k_0^2, \qquad k_0 = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}k_z = \sqrt{k_0^2 - (2\pi q)^2} = k_0\sqrt{1 - \lambda^2 q^2} \;\simeq\; k_0 - \tfrac12 k_0\lambda^2 q^2 = k_0 - \pi\lambda q^2
Over a distance z the component gains e^{\,i k_z z}. Dropping the carrier phase e^{\,i k_0 z} shared by every component:\boxed{H_z(q) = e^{-i\pi\lambda z q^2}}

Defocus records the wave Δf from the in-focus plane (underfocus: z = −Δf), so every q gets its own extra phase, growing as q²:\chi_{\text{def}}(q) = \pi\lambda\,\Delta f\, q^2Spherical aberration adds -\tfrac12\pi C_s\lambda^3 q^4, giving the χ(q) of the CTF (next slide)

slides.title: Each defocus value gives contrast to different spatial frequencies
slides.q: CTF(q) = sin χ(q), computed for 300 kV and Cₛ = 2.7 mm

items.title: Each defocus value gives contrast to different spatial frequencies
items.cap: Animation drawn for this deck from the content of the cryoEM slides; CTF computed live

points.text: Zeros: the image carries no information at those q. Negative lobes: contrast reversed
More defocus: stronger low-resolution contrast and faster oscillation
Collecting over a range of Δf puts the zeros at different q, so every q is measured somewhere
An envelope also damps high q: high resolution needs many averaged particles

slides.title: The forward model: from the 3D molecule to each recorded image

items.title: The forward model: from the 3D molecule to each recorded image
items.cap: Animation drawn for this deck from the content of the cryoEM slides; projection, CTF, shift and noise computed live

points.text: V(\mathbf r): the molecule’s 3D scattering potential, at each position \mathbf r
Particle i lies in the ice with its own orientation R_i
Projection (41): the beam adds up V along z, giving the 2D image P_{R_i}V
Fourier space (42): that image is a central slice \tilde V(R_i^{\mathsf T}\mathbf q) of the 3D transform
The CTF C_i(\mathbf q) multiplies every spatial frequency \mathbf q
A shift \mathbf t_i in the box is a phase ramp e^{-2\pi i\,\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf t_i}
Noise N_i(\mathbf q) on top gives the recorded image Y_i(\mathbf q)
So (42) models the projection of the 3D volume (scattering potential) onto the 2D images we record
Known: Y_i, the Fourier transform of each raw 2D particle image, and C_i, the CTF calculated at each q from χ(q)
Goal: find the pose (R_i,\mathbf t_i) of every particle and the volume V, the electron scattering potential into which we fit atomic models

slides.intro: With an understanding of the basics of image formation in cryoEM, we now move on to the key theoretical model that governs 3D structure determination from the 2D images we obtain from the microscope.

slides.title: Projection and orientation: what one particle image records
slides.q: What does the beam record, and why does each image need its own orientation R?

items.cap: Ian’s Manim clip 01: mathematical illustration in dimensionless units (each click plays the next beat)
Animation from the CryoSPARC guide (guide.cryosparc.com): rays striking objects on their way to the detector

points.text: Projection: the beam integrates the 3D potential along z, so one view cannot fix depth
A beam from another direction: the detector frame rotates to x′, y′, z′. The rotation R turns the particle so we always integrate along the beam (z′), whatever its direction
In a real sample, particles sit in the ice in every orientation, so the beam effectively strikes each one from a different direction: each image needs its own R

slides.intro: So what is the projection P_{R}V, and why do we include the orientation R in our model?

slides.title: Central slice theorem
slides.q: Each 2D Fourier image samples a central plane through the 3D Fourier volume

points.text: Projection. The image integrates the scattering potential V along the beam direction z. R is a rotation matrix, so changing R changes the direction the beam passes through the molecule(P_R V)(x,y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} V\big(R^{\mathsf T}(x,y,z)^{\mathsf T}\big)\,dz
The 3D Fourier transform of the potential:\tilde V(k_x,k_y,k_z) = \iiint V(x,y,z)\,e^{-2\pi i\,(k_x x + k_y y + k_z z)}\,dx\,dy\,dz
The 2D Fourier transform of a projection (R = I, beam along z):\mathcal F_2\{PV\}(q_x,q_y) = \iint \Big[\int V(x,y,z)\,dz\Big]\, e^{-2\pi i\,(q_x x + q_y y)}\,dx\,dy

The exponential does not depend on z, so it moves inside the z-integral: this is the 3D transform with kz = 0\mathcal F_2\{PV\}(q_x,q_y) = \iiint V(x,y,z)\,e^{-2\pi i\,(q_x x + q_y y + 0\cdot z)}\,dx\,dy\,dz = \tilde V(q_x,q_y,0)

So the 2D transform of a projection is the plane through the origin of the 3D transform, perpendicular to the beam. For any orientation R the plane simply rotates:\mathcal F_2\{P_R V\}(\mathbf q) = \tilde V\big(R^{\mathsf T}(q_x,q_y,0)^{\mathsf T}\big)

Consequence: every particle image fills one central plane of V̂. Images from many orientations fill the 3D Fourier volume, and an inverse 3D transform gives back V (next slide); orientations clustered around one axis leave a missing cone unmeasured

slides.intro:
Here we want to express our projected 2D image in reciprocal (Fourier) space.

This is because, as we saw, CTF(q) adds a different relative phase shift to the components at each spatial frequency q.

slides.title: The forward model in Fourier space: CTF, shift and noise

items.title: The CTF, shift and noise terms of the forward model
items.cap: Animation drawn for this deck from the content of the cryoEM slides; images computed live

points.text: Recall the forward model (42): every term is a function of the spatial frequency \mathbf q
The CTF C_i(\mathbf q) is a simple product in Fourier space
Why Fourier space pays offSo now that we have expressed our 2D projection in Fourier space, we can directly multiply it by the CTF Ci(q), the term that carries the defocus phase shift χ(q).
But how exactly do the shift \mathbf t_i and the noise N_i(\mathbf q) make sense here?
Two Fourier properties: a shift becomes a phase factor, a convolution becomes a product
e^{-2\pi i\,\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf t_i} is just the in-plane shift \mathbf t_i of the particle in real space, written in Fourier space
So the pose (R_i,\mathbf t_i) says where exactly each particle is (\mathbf t_i) and how it is oriented relative to the beam (R_i)
Noise N_i(\mathbf q) is taken to be Gaussian, as assumed throughout the literature

slides.title: Reconstruction, known poses (1/2): a linear Gaussian model
slides.q: If every pose (Rᵢ, tᵢ) were known, how would we recover the map V?

\Sigma_i,\ |\Sigma_i|,\ \Sigma_i^{-1}noise covariance of image i; its determinant; its inverse
p(\mathbf y_i\mid\mathbf v)likelihood: probability of image i if the map were v

points.text: With every pose known, the forward model in real space (the voxels of V stacked into one vector v) is linear: \mathbf y_i = A_i\,\mathbf v + \boldsymbol\varepsilon_i, where Ai (rotate, project, shift, CTF-filter) is a fixed matrix

The residual \mathbf y_i - A_i\mathbf v is the recorded image minus its prediction A_i\mathbf v. If v is the true map, the residual is exactly the noise:\mathbf y_i - A_i\mathbf v = \boldsymbol\varepsilon_i, \qquad \boldsymbol\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal N(\mathbf 0, \Sigma_i)

One pixel: the noise \varepsilon \sim \mathcal N(0,\sigma^2) has the standard Gaussian density. A measurement y = \mu + \varepsilon is then as probable as its noise, so evaluate that density at the residual y - \mu:p(\varepsilon) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\,e^{-\varepsilon^2/2\sigma^2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p(y\mid\mu) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\,e^{-(y-\mu)^2/2\sigma^2}

m pixels, independent noise \Sigma = \mathrm{diag}(\sigma_1^2,\dots,\sigma_m^2): multiply the m one-pixel densities. The normalisers multiply to (2\pi)^{m/2}|\Sigma|^{1/2} and the exponents add:p(\mathbf y\mid\boldsymbol\mu) = \prod_{j=1}^{m}\frac{e^{-(y_j-\mu_j)^2/2\sigma_j^2}}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma_j^2}} = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{m/2}|\Sigma|^{1/2}}\exp\Big[-\tfrac12\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{(y_j-\mu_j)^2}{\sigma_j^2}\Big]and the sum is (\mathbf y-\boldsymbol\mu)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf y-\boldsymbol\mu), which also covers correlated pixels (any Σ)

Set μ = Aiv, the prediction, to get the likelihood of image i given the map:\boxed{\;p(\mathbf y_i\mid\mathbf v) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{m/2}|\Sigma_i|^{1/2}}\exp\Big[-\tfrac12\,(\mathbf y_i-A_i\mathbf v)^{\mathsf T}\,\Sigma_i^{-1}\,(\mathbf y_i-A_i\mathbf v)\Big]\;}The exponent is the noise-weighted squared residual, and v enters only through it: the closer the prediction is to the image, the more probable the image

slides.intro:
So how do we recover the 3D volume V (i.e. reconstruction) in practice? First, let us assume we know one of the two unknowns: the pose (Ri, ti).

Expressing the forward equation in real space (inverse 2D transform \mathcal F_2^{-1}, with the voxels of V stacked into one vector v), we have:\underbrace{\mathbf y_i}_{\mathcal F_2^{-1}[Y_i]} \;=\; \underbrace{A_i\,\mathbf v}_{\mathcal F_2^{-1}\left[C_i\,\tilde V(R_i^{\mathsf T}[q_x,q_y,0]^{\mathsf T})\,e^{-2\pi i\,\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf t_i}\right]} \;+\; \underbrace{\boldsymbol\varepsilon_i}_{\mathcal F_2^{-1}[N_i]}With the pose and CTF known, Ai is a fixed matrix: the problem is linear in v.

slides.title: Reconstruction, known poses (2/2): the normal equations
slides.q: Maximum likelihood: which map v makes all N images most probable?

aside.html:
Terms
Nnumber of particle images
p(\mathbf y_i\mid\mathbf v)likelihood: probability of image i if the map were v
L(\mathbf v)negative log-likelihood (the misfit to minimize)
\Sigma_i^{-1}precision matrix: down-weights noisy pixels
A_i^{\mathsf T}back-projection: smears a 2D image back into 3D
\nabla_{\mathbf v}gradient with respect to the voxels of v
\hat{\mathbf v}maximum-likelihood estimate of the map
\text{const}terms independent of v (e.g. the normalizer of each Gaussian)

points.text: The N images are independent given v, so the joint likelihood is a product:p(\mathbf y_1,\dots,\mathbf y_N\mid\mathbf v) = \prod_{i=1}^{N} p(\mathbf y_i\mid\mathbf v)

A product of thousands of tiny probabilities is numerically unstable; the log turns it into a sum, \log\prod_i p_i = \sum_i \log\, p_i. Keeping only the terms that depend on v:-\log\, p(\mathbf y_1,\dots,\mathbf y_N\mid\mathbf v) = L(\mathbf v) + \text{const}, \qquad L(\mathbf v) = \frac12\sum_{i=1}^{N}(\mathbf y_i-A_i\mathbf v)^{\mathsf T}\,\Sigma_i^{-1}\,(\mathbf y_i-A_i\mathbf v)Maximizing the likelihood = minimizing L, a noise-weighted least-squares misfit
Take the gradient with respect to v:\nabla_{\mathbf v} L = \sum_{i=1}^{N} A_i^{\mathsf T}\,\Sigma_i^{-1}\,(A_i\mathbf v-\mathbf y_i)

Setting \nabla_{\mathbf v} L = \mathbf 0 gives the normal equations, which are solved for the estimate \hat{\mathbf v}:\boxed{\;\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{N} A_i^{\mathsf T}\,\Sigma_i^{-1}A_i\Big)\,\hat{\mathbf v} \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{N} A_i^{\mathsf T}\,\Sigma_i^{-1}\,\mathbf y_i\;}Right: every image back-projected into 3D, weighted by its noise. Left: how often each part of v was measured. Solving divides one by the other

slides.title: Reconstruction, unknown poses: alternate poses and map
slides.q: Neither the poses nor the map is known: alternate between them until both stop changing

aside.html:
Terms
\phi_i = (R_i,\mathbf t_i)pose of particle i, now an unknown
A(\phi)the projection matrix for pose φ (same as Ai)
SO(3)\times\mathbb R^2all 3D rotations × all in-plane shifts
\|\mathbf r\|^2_{\Sigma^{-1}}\mathbf r^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf r: noise-weighted squared misfit
\mathbf v^{(0)}initial volume
kiteration number
\mathbf v^{(k)},\ \phi_i^{(k)}map and poses after iteration k
\arg\minthe value that minimizes the expression

points.text: Now the map v and every pose \phi_i = (R_i,\mathbf t_i) are unknown. The same misfit, with A_i = A(\phi_i), is minimized over both:\min_{\mathbf v,\ \phi_1,\dots,\phi_N}\; L(\mathbf v,\phi_1,\dots,\phi_N) = \frac12\sum_{i=1}^{N}\big\|\mathbf y_i - A(\phi_i)\,\mathbf v\big\|^2_{\Sigma_i^{-1}}A(φ) is nonlinear in the pose, so there is no closed-form solution
Start from an initial volume \mathbf v^{(0)} (ab initio, or a low-pass filtered reference), then repeat for k = 0, 1, 2, …
Pose step: hold the map, give each image its best pose\phi_i^{(k)} = \arg\min_{\phi\,\in\,SO(3)\times\mathbb R^2}\ \big\|\mathbf y_i - A(\phi)\,\mathbf v^{(k)}\big\|^2_{\Sigma_i^{-1}}

Map step: hold the poses and solve the known-pose problem (normal equations)\Big(\sum_{i} A(\phi_i^{(k)})^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_i^{-1}A(\phi_i^{(k)})\Big)\,\mathbf v^{(k+1)} = \sum_{i} A(\phi_i^{(k)})^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_i^{-1}\,\mathbf y_i

Stop when L no longer decreases. Neither step can raise L, so the loop converges, but to a local optimum that depends on \mathbf v^{(0)}. RELION and CryoSPARC soften the pose step: they weight every pose by its probability (expectation–maximization) instead of keeping only the best one

slides.title: Reconstruction, unknown poses: the loop in action
slides.q: Can the poses and the map be found together from noisy images alone?

items.title: Reconstruction, unknown poses: the loop in action
items.cap: Animation drawn for this deck from the content of the cryoEM slides; 100 simulated images, alignment computed live

points.text: 2D toy: every image \mathbf y_i is the same object rotated by an unknown angle \phi_i, plus heavy noise. Start from a blurred blob \mathbf v^{(0)}
Pose step: compare each image with \mathbf v^{(0)} rotated through every angle (5° steps); the best match is its pose. The images turn to their estimated poses
Map step: rotate the images back and average them → \mathbf v^{(1)}. Already far clearer than any single image
Repeat: a better map gives better poses, and better poses a better map. The mean pose error falls from 22° to ≈ 2° within two iterations
Compare with the truth: the same object, up to an overall rotation that the images alone can never fix. A poor \mathbf v^{(0)} can trap the loop in a local optimum

explain.text: J1, Import Particle Stack loads the particle images from a .star file: 5,000 particles in one output group (right). The low-pass filtered previews (centre) show straight filament segments lying in every in-plane direction.

The warnings say the file has no orientations (no rlnAngleRot, Tilt, Psi): the poses (Ri, ti) are what must be found. The log lists what each particle does carry: a 160 × 160 px box at 5.76 Å/px, and its CTF parameters (defocus, amplitude contrast 0.1), so J2 can apply Ci(q).

J2, Ab-initio Reconstruction uses all 5,000 particles, 1 class and no assumed symmetry (C1). It starts from a random map and alternates pose and map steps, the loop of the previous slides; the slider shows iteration 900.

By iteration 900, three central slices through the map and the volume preview (top) show a filament; the log reports a resolution of ≈ 17 Å. I stopped the job after 8 min 17 s: enough for a first map.
